original_value: Blue noise sampling has proved useful for many graphics applications, but remains underexplored in high-dimensional spaces due to the difficulty of generating distributions and proving properties about them. We present a blue noise sampling method with good quality and performance across different dimensions. The method, spoke-dart sampling, shoots rays from prior samples and selects samples from these rays. It combines the advantages of two major high-dimensional sampling methods: the locality of advancing front with the dimensionality-reduction of hyperplanes, specifically line sampling. We prove that the output sampling is saturated with high probability, with bounds on distances between pairs of samples and between any domain point and its nearest sample. We demonstrate spoke-dart applications for approximate Delaunay graph construction, global optimization, and robotic motion planning. Both the blue-noise quality of the output distribution and the adaptability of the intermediate processes of our method are useful in these applications.

result.paraphrase: Blue noise sampling has proven useful in many graphics applications, yet it remains underexplored in high-dimensional spaces because generating such distributions and proving their properties is difficult. We introduce a blue-noise sampling method that delivers strong quality and performance across dimensions. Called spoke-dart sampling, it casts rays from existing samples and chooses new samples from those rays. The method combines two key high-dimensional sampling ideas: the locality of advancing front and the dimensionality reduction of hyperplanes, namely line sampling. We prove that the resulting sample set is saturated with high probability, with bounds on the distances between pairs of samples and between any point in the domain and its nearest sample. We show spoke-dart applications in approximate Delaunay graph construction, global optimization, and robotic motion planning. In these applications, both the blue-noise quality of the output distribution and the adaptability of the method’s intermediate processes are beneficial.
